If there are enemy fighters present in the air zone where the naval strike or port strike is taking place, they can engage in ⟦0⟧ and potentially disrupt the bombers before they even reach their ship targets. See the dedicated article on ⟦1⟧ for more information.

The naval strike target of an undisrupted bomber wing is randomly selected from a weighted distribution of all enemy ships. The base weight is each ship's maximum HP, excluding hidden submarines. This gets scaled depending on ship type:

The weight of damaged ships gets increased by up to ⟦0⟧ as they approach 0% HP. If a ship's anti-air (AA) attack is below 5,⟦1⟧ the weight is increased by ⟦2⟧. For example, convoys have only 0.2 AA attack, increasing their score by 5 * (5 - 0.2) = ⟦3⟧.

It can potentially be a viable strategy to deliberately have low amounts of AA on certain ships, potentially even no AA. When operating alongside more valuable ships that have a high weight of being selected for naval attack, e.g., fleet carriers, less valuable ships with low to no AA can potentially draw attention away from these valuable ships, thus increasing those ships' survivability at the cost of their own.

Phase 3: Naval strike attack and damage

The ship's speed and armor do not matter in this case.

Critical hits are calculated the same way as for a ship's torpedo. See ⟦0⟧ for more information.
If the naval battle was a port strike, the naval base gets damaged proportionately to the damage dealt against the ship.

It is important to note that the AA of the targeted ship counts ⟦0⟧ more for AA damage reduction purposes than ships in the rest of the fleet, and that the damage reduction effect increases very slowly with additional AA thanks to the exponent in the formula. This makes AA far less valuable on ships that are not expected to be targeted by enemy aircraft, e.g., screening ships in a battle fleet composed of larger capital ships and/or carriers.

When a naval battle starts, screens can only attack after ⟦0⟧ hours, and capital ships can only attack after ⟦1⟧ hours, but carriers can attack from hour ⟦2⟧.⟦3⟧ This coincides with the 6⟦4⟧ hours referred to as the 'Initial Stage' by modifiers like the ⟦5⟧ ⟦6⟧ spirit. It also lines up with carrier aircraft being able to sortie every 6⟦7⟧ hours (OBSOLETE, it is currently 8 hours, starting close to high noon), though they are unable to sortie at night without something like the ⟦8⟧ ⟦9⟧ spirit.

For a fleet with a far more significant carrier force compared to the enemy fleet, these opening, carrier-only combat stages can produce a devastating alpha strike that can start a snowball effect of the enemy fleet dealing less damage as a result of reduced organization, which then causes their organization to fall faster than the allied fleets', reducing their damage even further. However, if the battle starts at night or in a ⟦0⟧, this initial stage can be wasted because carrier traffic will be severely reduced or non-existent during the stage.

It is important to note that while carriers can have light attack from equipping ⟦0⟧, carriers will not use their light attack to fire at ships in the enemy carrier group/line. This includes enemy carriers, but also enemy convoys. Among other things, this makes 'battlecarrier' designs (heavily armored carrier designs bristling with light attack, sacrificing deck space) even less effective than what one might expect, especially at ⟦1⟧.

Like other ships, carriers can gain (or lose) ⟦0⟧, leading to them gaining or losing veterancy levels that can give various bonuses and penalties. Unlike other ships, however, carriers do not receive any benefits to their damage from veterancy levels, receiving sortie efficiency penalties and bonuses instead.

Instead, it is the carrier air wings stationed on carriers whose ⟦0⟧ levels and veterancy can affect the damage by carriers. Especially as newly deployed air wings start at ⟦1⟧ veterancy, and because carrier-based air wings can lose veterancy in naval battles very quickly because of how much bigger losses are relative to their wing size, it can be very important to train air wings stationed on carriers before sending them into engagements. ⟦2⟧ can also be assigned to carrier air wings and affect their combat performance.

⟦0⟧ dictates what percentage of the aircraft on a given carrier can actually fly in both ⟦1⟧ and during naval battles. Carriers have a base sortie efficiency of ⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧ with doctrines like ⟦4⟧ and ⟦5⟧ being the main source of increases to it. ⟦6⟧ and ⟦7⟧ doctrines are able to provide up to ⟦8⟧ additional sortie efficiency, while ⟦9⟧ doctrines can provide a full ⟦10⟧. Political advisors, national spirits, ⟦11⟧, admiral ⟦12⟧, and admiral traits like ⟦13⟧ and ⟦14⟧ can all provide additional sortie efficiency, as can having full ⟦15⟧. Sortie efficiency of over 100% does not make existing planes more effective, so it does nothing unless the carrier is overcrowded.

Carriers have a maximum capacity for aircraft and, similar to land-based ⟦0⟧, this capacity can be exceeded at the cost of a ⟦1⟧ penalty to how many aircraft can actually fly from the carrier for every ⟦2⟧ that its deck space is exceeded. Overcrowding penalties can be reduced directly by the ⟦3⟧ naval doctrine, but they can also be mitigated and even outright negated by having a sortie efficiency of over 100%.

For example, if a carrier has deck space for 80 aircraft, but is hosting 10 air wings of 10 aircraft each for a total of 100 aircraft, it would normally be exceeding its capacity by ⟦0⟧, thus reducing the amount of aircraft that can sortie from it by ⟦1⟧. With ⟦2⟧ total sortie efficiency, only ⟦3⟧ of its 100 aircraft = ⟦4⟧ aircraft could fly. However, if the carrier has ⟦5⟧ total sortie efficiency through various sources, it is able to sortie ⟦6⟧ more aircraft than normal. The two effects counteract each other, allowing ⟦7⟧ of the carrier's 100 aircraft = ⟦8⟧ aircraft to fly.

Each carrier exceeding ⟦0⟧⟦1⟧ per side causes ⟦2⟧ of that side's carrier wings to be unable to target enemy ships in naval battles. This scales up to ⟦3⟧ of that side's carrier wings being unable to target ships. The number of wings that are able to target enemy ships is always rounded down, and unlike other penalties affecting carrier wings, each carrier plane type counts as a single wing for this penalty. The penalty is different from sortie efficiency, which affects the mission efficiency of carrier-based planes based on how many planes there are stationed on a single carrier. Aircraft that are unable to target enemy ships will still fly, allowing them to get shot down by enemy fighters.
As carrier-based fighters never target ships, this penalty never affects carrier-based fighters.

The penalty is applied to carriers from the bottom of the ship list upwards, meaning air wings from carriers near or at the top of the list are more likely to be able to target enemy ships than those at or near the bottom. Fighter air wings on any carrier will always operate as though the penalty does not exist, so when expecting to have more than ⟦0⟧ carriers in a single naval battle, it is better to put fighter air wings on the carriers listed lower in the task force and naval bomber air wings on the carriers listed at the top of the task force's ship list.

In general, this penalty also generally discourages fielding lots of cheaper escort carriers (carriers with just one or two hangar spaces, usually converted from outdated cruisers), as -998 or more escort carriers will suffer the same penalties as the same number of full carriers, even though the escort carriers have far less deck space than the full carriers.
You have 6 carriers in a battle with the following air wings ordered in the following way:
Carrier 6: 1x 10 Carrier Bombers, 1x 10 Carrier Close Air Support, 1x 10 Carrier Fighters

With 6 carriers, the carrier overstacking penalty prevents -100399500% of all carrier wings from targeting enemy ships, rounded down. For this penalty, the first four carriers count as having only 1 air wing each. The 5th carrier counts as having 2 air wings and the 6th carrier counts as having 3 air wings. This gives a total of 9 carrier air wings. -100399500% of 9 is 9035964 air wings, and which rounds down to 9035964 air wings that can target enemy ships. These wings are counted from those based on the first carrier in the list going downward. This means that the naval bombers on the first 5 carriers will operate as normal, while the naval bombers and CAS on carrier number 6 will not launch attacks at enemy ships, but they will still take off and be vulnerable to enemy fighters. The carrier fighters on carriers number 5 and 6 are unaffected by the penalty, and so will fly and can target enemy aircraft regardless.

In order to be able to base aircraft on an aircraft carrier, carrier capable models must be produced. When playing without ⟦0⟧ and its ⟦1⟧, the land-based version of an aircraft must first be researched, then the carrier-capable version is researched separately. This is done by clicking the aircraft carrier button on the aircraft type in the air research tab. This can only be done for Fighters, Close Air Support, and Naval Bombers. The carrier-capable version has a different model name than the land-based version, as well as different artwork and different stats. If you don't intend to use aircraft carriers, you do not need to research carrier-capable planes.
With ⟦0⟧'s ⟦1⟧, researching any light airframe also grants access to its carrier-capable version, from which a buildable variant (fighter, naval bomber, or CAS) may be created.

When a new carrier is produced, the planes that will be based on it by default can be customized as part of the carrier production line in the naval section using dockyards. Once finished, the carrier will be filled by the most up-to-date models that are available in the country's stockpile. Replacements and reinforcements to these wings will need to be produced using ⟦0⟧ and can otherwise be manipulated by first selecting the carrier(s) and then clicking the little airplane button next to their location on the map, similar to a land-based ⟦1⟧.

When an aircraft carrier is part of a fleet that is on patrol in one or more regions, then the wings based on it are shown as on a carrier mission. They will operate as a Carrier Air Group and automatically take part in any naval combat that the fleet engages in. There is no need to give them any specific orders if they are intended to be used in this way.
